name: Back extension / deadlift strength

angle.text: Looksmaxxers pair deadlifts and back extensions with posture goals, aiming for a stronger upper back and spinal erectors so they stand and sit more upright and carry a fuller, wider-looking back. The lifts are well-established strength training; their effect on posture appearance specifically has not been trialled.

summary: Posterior-chain lifting (deadlifts, back extensions) that looksmaxxers pair with posture goals; well-established strength training, but no trials on appearance.
note: Rounding the back under heavy load is described as controversial and as a possible injury factor; no appearance-specific trials were found.
currentQuick:
The deadlift lifts a weight from the floor to hip level and is one of the three powerlifting lifts. The back extension is a bodyweight or weighted exercise that works the erector spinae muscles along the spine. Both are used in strength training to build the muscles of the back of the body.
In posture and looksmaxxing discussions they are framed as ways to build a stronger back and hips. Wikipedia describes the mechanics and muscles involved but not research on posture or appearance, and no trial found tests either exercise for those outcomes.
How it works: The conventional deadlift mainly works the glutes, with the quadriceps, hamstrings, trapezius, lats and erector spinae contributing. Back extensions target the erector spinae (spinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis) and, in reverse-hyperextension machines, the glutes and part of the hamstrings.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia lists rounding the back as a common error, calling it controversial and saying excessive rounding may lead to injury. Trap-bar versions are described as generally less taxing on the lower back. Back extension guidance on the same source advises lighter loads for beginners to avoid straining the back.
deepLead:
The deadlift is a strength exercise in which a weight is lifted from the ground to hip level and lowered again, most often with a barbell. It is one of the three powerlifting lifts and a signature strongman event. The back extension, also called hyperextension, strengthens the erector spinae muscles through arching the spine back from a bent-forward position, performed on a Roman chair, 45-degree bench or reverse-hyperextension machine or with no equipment.
Looksmaxxing and posture communities discuss both under the heading of posterior chain strength. Published encyclopedic sources describe the muscles worked and variations, but no clinical trial was identified testing these exercises for posture, back-muscle appearance or facial and body aesthetics.

name: Yoga for posture

angle.text: People use postural yoga to loosen tight chest and hip areas and build awareness of alignment, with the aim of standing taller and more open. Studies cover back pain and stress; its effect on visible posture or looks has been tested very little.

summary: Postural yoga used for mobility and alignment; some evidence for back pain and stress, little direct testing on posture or looks.
note: Inverted poses such as headstand have been linked in case reports to raised eye pressure and glaucoma progression.
currentQuick:
Modern postural yoga combines stretches, strength holds and breathing and is widely practised as exercise. Posture and mobility communities recommend it for flexibility and body awareness.
Reviews summarised on Wikipedia report moderate-quality evidence that yoga reduces back pain, and small studies report stress reduction. The sources found include no controlled trial of yoga changing standing posture or visible appearance.
How it works: Proponents say holding stretched and supported positions improves flexibility, strength and body awareness. One 2017 study mapped core muscle activation across different yoga postures, giving a muscular basis for strength claims.
Risks and caveats: Case reports describe glaucomatous optic nerve damage progressing in people who regularly practised the headstand, with eye pressure rising in the head-down position. Wikipedia's overview of yoga as exercise cites health claims but notes the field is understudied.
deepLead:
Yoga for posture refers to using yoga asanas (physical poses) to improve flexibility, strength and alignment. Modern postural yoga was developed in the early twentieth century, revived in the 1920s by teachers such as Yogendra and Kuvalayananda and spread by students of Tirumalai Krishnamacharya, including B.K.S. Iyengar, whose Light on Yoga (1966) helped popularise it worldwide.
Evidence is strongest for back pain: reviews cited on Wikipedia, including a 2017 review, report moderate-quality evidence that yoga reduces back pain. Small experimental studies show stress-reduction effects of short yoga sessions. No trial found has tested yoga for changing standing posture or appearance.

name: Pilates

angle.text: Pilates is used in posture and fitness circles to build core control and a more upright, toned look. Reviews show back-pain benefit similar to other exercise; direct data on posture appearance is limited.

summary: Core-focused mind-body exercise system used for posture and tone; reviews find back-pain benefit comparable to other exercise, with little direct posture-appearance data.
note: Evidence reviews describe benefit for low back pain similar to other exercise; it has not been shown to treat medical conditions.
currentQuick:
Pilates is a low-impact exercise system developed by Joseph Pilates in the early twentieth century, originally called Contrology. It stresses controlled movement, breathing and core engagement, on a mat or on spring-based apparatus such as the Reformer.
In posture and body-aesthetics communities it is used for core conditioning and alignment. Reviews cited on Wikipedia describe low-quality evidence that it beats no exercise for low back pain but is no better than other exercise, and no trial found tests it for appearance.
How it works: Proponents say deliberate control of the trunk muscles, the so-called powerhouse, improves stability, alignment and body awareness. Network meta-analyses of back-pain exercise include Pilates among effective exercise types.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia and the sources reviewed describe low-impact exercise with no discussion of significant harms. Grokipedia and Wikipedia note Pilates has not been shown to be an effective treatment for any medical condition.
deepLead:
Pilates is a mind-body exercise system named for Joseph Pilates, who developed it in the first half of the twentieth century and called it Contrology. He said the idea arose during his World War I internment on the Isle of Man, and published Your Health (1934) and Return to Life Through Contrology (1945). It emphasises core stability, breathing, alignment and flexibility, performed on a mat or on apparatus such as the Reformer and Cadillac.
A systematic review noted the difficulty of defining Pilates exercise consistently across studies. Network meta-analyses of exercise for chronic low back pain include Pilates among effective modes, and Wikipedia reports low-quality evidence that it beats no exercise but is no better than other exercise. No study found tests Pilates for changing posture appearance.

name: Feldenkrais Method

angle.text: Followers use Feldenkrais lessons to become aware of habitual tension and movement patterns, with the hope of carrying themselves more easily and upright. Reviews have not found conclusive benefit, and its effect on how posture looks has not been tested.

summary: Gentle somatic movement education aimed at body awareness and efficient movement; reviews find no conclusive evidence of medical benefit, and posture looks are untested.
note: Reviews report no conclusive evidence of medical benefit; researchers do not consider it to pose serious risks.
currentQuick:
The Feldenkrais Method is a movement-education system created by Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). It is taught in verbally guided group classes (Awareness Through Movement) and one-to-one hands-on sessions (Functional Integration).
Proponents say it improves awareness and ease of movement, and it is sometimes mentioned in posture discussions. Reviews describe no conclusive evidence of medical benefit, with some small trials in chronic low back pain; no study found tests it for appearance.
How it works: Proponents say slow, exploratory movement and attention to sensation help the nervous system learn new movement patterns. Some researchers link the method to dynamic systems theory of motor behaviour.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia says researchers do not believe the method poses serious risks. Critics, including physician David Gorski, have compared it to faith healing, and Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness.
deepLead:
The Feldenkrais Method is a form of somatic education devised by Israeli physicist and judo expert Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). Its two formats are Awareness Through Movement, verbally guided group lessons, and Functional Integration, hands-on individual sessions. Proponents claim it improves movement quality and awareness and repairs brain-body connections.
Reviews report no conclusive evidence of medical benefit. A 2015 Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness and in 2017 it was excluded from private health insurance subsidies, according to Wikipedia. Small randomised trials in chronic low back pain exist, and systematic reviews have assessed its use as a physiotherapy tool. No study found tests it for posture appearance.

name: Rolfing / structural integration

angle.text: Rolfing is promoted as a ten-session bodywork series that lengthens connective tissue and realigns the body, which clients hope gives a taller, more balanced posture. The posture-change claim rests largely on practitioner accounts, with little controlled research.

summary: Ten-session fascial bodywork for posture and alignment; reviews find little good evidence for its claims.
note: Deep tissue work can be painful; caution advised with cancer.
currentQuick:
Rolfing is a hands-on bodywork system created by Ida Rolf, delivered as a ten-session series that manipulates fascia while guiding movement. It is promoted for posture, alignment, pain and stress.
The research base is small. Reviews cited by encyclopedias describe the evidence as very low certainty or absent, and no study tests appearance outcomes.
How it works: Practitioners apply sustained manual pressure to connective tissue with the aim of lengthening it and re-aligning the body with gravity, accompanied by movement education.
Risks and caveats: Sessions can be painful and leave soreness. Safety has not been formally confirmed, and deep tissue work is a concern for people with cancer. It is largely unlicensed, and Australia removed it from insurance subsidies in 2017.
deepLead:
Rolfing, also called structural integration, is a form of manual bodywork developed by the biochemist Ida Rolf (1896-1979). Practitioners apply slow, sustained pressure to the body's connective tissue (fascia) combined with movement cues, with the stated aim of lengthening tissue and aligning the body with gravity . It is usually delivered as a series of ten sessions .
Proponents describe benefits including better posture and movement, less pain and stress reduction. Encyclopedia sources describe the alignment-based claims as not established by scientific studies, and a 2015 Australian government review of alternative therapies found no clear evidence of effectiveness for Rolfing . Within appearance culture it is mentioned as a route to "fixing" posture and body alignment.

name: Chiropractic adjustments

angle.text: Some people seek chiropractic adjustments hoping to straighten the spine and improve posture and frame. Trials have looked at back and neck pain with low-certainty benefit; lasting posture or appearance change has not been shown.

summary: Chiropractic spinal manipulation: some low-certainty benefit for back and neck pain, little evidence for posture or appearance claims.
note: Neck manipulation has been linked to rare vertebral artery stroke; causality is disputed.
currentQuick:
Chiropractic adjustments are quick manual thrusts to spinal joints, used mainly for back and neck pain and promoted in posture circles for alignment.
Reviews report small or low-certainty benefits for some back and neck pain and no good evidence for non-musculoskeletal conditions. No study was found testing aesthetic outcomes.
How it works: A practitioner applies a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust to a spinal joint. Chiropractic theory attributes effects to correcting subluxations, a concept described as unsubstantiated.
Risks and caveats: Soreness and headache are common and temporary. Rare serious events, including stroke after neck manipulation, are reported, with causality debated. The profession is licensed in most places.
deepLead:
A chiropractic adjustment is a manual intervention, most often a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, applied to the joints of the spine; chiropractors use "adjustment" for what clinical literature calls spinal manipulation . It is the core technique of chiropractic, a profession founded in the 1890s by D. D. Palmer .
It is most often used for back and neck pain. In appearance and posture communities it is discussed as a way to correct alignment or "reset" the spine. Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest or low-certainty benefits for some back and neck pain and no good evidence for non-musculoskeletal conditions, while safety discussions centre on rare serious events after neck manipulation .

name: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) cervical lordosis

chain: Traction and exercise on the neck
angle.text: CBP is used by people with forward head posture who want to restore the neck's natural curve for a better side profile and neck line. Supporting studies come mostly from CBP-affiliated researchers, and looks outcomes are not measured.

summary: Chiropractic traction and exercise system aiming to restore the neck curve; evidence is mostly from CBP-affiliated studies.
note: Relies on spinal X-rays; evidence mostly from affiliated authors.
currentQuick:
CBP is a chiropractic system that tries to restore the neck's forward curve (cervical lordosis) using traction, exercises and adjustments.
Most supporting studies come from CBP-affiliated authors, and critics question whether curve changes relate to symptoms.
How it works: Practitioners measure curves on X-rays and apply sustained extension traction, orthotics and Mirror Image positioning intended to produce lasting tissue change.
Risks and caveats: Repeated X-rays add radiation exposure, and neck manipulation has been associated with rare stroke. Certification is voluntary.
deepLead:
Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) is a posture-focused chiropractic technique founded in 1980 by Donald Harrison, Deanne Harrison and Daniel Murphy. It uses mathematical models of ideal spinal curves, and combines adjustments, exercises and traction to try to restore them . Cervical lordosis, the natural forward curve of the neck, is one of its main targets.
Proponents claim that restoring the curve reduces pain and improves posture. Grokipedia, which draws mainly on CBP-affiliated sources, describes a body of mostly CBP-authored studies, while noting critics who question whether curve deviations relate to symptoms and point to weak study designs .

name: Physiotherapy for posture

angle.text: People see a physiotherapist to correct forward head posture or rounded shoulders using exercise and guidance. Physical therapy is well established for movement problems; posture changes judged by appearance have limited study.

summary: Supervised corrective exercise for posture; general physio is well established, posture-for-looks evidence is thin.
note: Link between specific postures and health outcomes is weak per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
A licensed physiotherapist prescribes exercises and manual therapy to change habits like forward head posture.
Physical therapy is established for many musculoskeletal problems, but little evidence addresses posture for appearance.
How it works: Strengthening of weak muscles, stretching of tight ones, mobilization and ergonomic changes.
Risks and caveats: Generally low risk when delivered by licensed practitioners; cost and effort are the main community complaints.
deepLead:
Physiotherapy for posture refers to supervised exercise, manual therapy and education from a licensed physical therapist aimed at changing habitual alignment such as forward head posture or rounded shoulders . Physical therapy is a regulated healthcare profession that treats movement limitations, with exercise as a core tool .
Evidence that physical therapy improves pain and function in many musculoskeletal conditions is described in encyclopedias . Wikipedia also states there is little strong evidence that any particular posture leads to better medical outcomes .

name: Postural Restoration Institute (PRI)

angle.text: PRI-trained therapists teach breathing and positional exercises aimed at correcting asymmetries, which users hope leads to a more even, neutral posture. There is little published trial evidence for the approach, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

summary: Therapist-taught breathing and asymmetry exercise system for posture; little published trial evidence.
note: Evidence base is mostly case reports and physiology papers.
currentQuick:
PRI is a posture method from physical therapist Ron Hruska built around breathing and body asymmetry.
The evidence base is thin, mostly case reports and basic physiology.
How it works: Specific breathing and positioning exercises aim to reduce asymmetric patterns and reposition the ribcage and pelvis.
Risks and caveats: Not documented in the sources reviewed; delivered by licensed professionals.
deepLead:
Postural Restoration is a posture-based approach to physical medicine developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska in the early 1990s. In 1999 he founded the Postural Restoration Institute in Lincoln, Nebraska, to train health professionals . It uses manual and non-manual exercises to reposition and retrain the body toward neutral alignment .
Advocates claim it improves alignment, breathing mechanics and asymmetrical movement patterns. Wikipedia states there is little strong evidence that any specific posture leads to better medical outcomes .

name: Kinesiology tape posture taping

chain: Less rounded shoulders and forward head
Better side profile and neck line
angle.text: Posture communities use elastic tape across the upper back as a reminder to hold the shoulders back, aiming for a better profile and neck line. Evidence on the tape concerns pain, and its use for posture appearance is untested.

summary: Elastic tape across the upper back as a shoulder-position reminder; the tape's pain evidence is thin and posture-for-looks is untested.
note: No studies found on taping for posture or appearance.
currentQuick:
Posture taping means sticking elastic kinesiology tape across the shoulders and upper back so that you feel a tug when your shoulders slump. Some people use it hoping for a straighter, more open posture.
The tape was developed in the 1970s and became famous at the Olympics. Reviews of it for pain and performance report small effects, and no study among those found tests it for posture appearance.
How it works: The idea is sensory feedback: the tape pulls on the skin when posture slips, which proponents say improves body awareness. Manufacturers have also claimed effects on fascia and lymph flow, which critics say lack evidence.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks are minor and not detailed in the available sources; skin irritation from adhesive is a general consideration. In 2017 the leading brand settled a lawsuit over marketing claims.
deepLead:
Kinesiology tape posture taping is the use of stretchy, adhesive elastic tape, commonly sold as Kinesio tape or K-tape, across the shoulders and upper back to cue a more upright shoulder position. In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is discussed as a way to counter rounded shoulders and forward-head posture, which people link to a more favorable side profile and neck line.
The tape itself is a thin cotton strip with acrylic adhesive that can stretch to roughly 140% of its length and is marketed for pain and sports injuries. It was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and became widely visible after it was supplied to athletes at the 2008 and 2012 Olympics .
Systematic reviews of kinesiology tape for pain and performance have generally reported small or trivial effects and little advantage over other treatments or sham taping, as summarized on Wikipedia . Sources available for this article do not include a controlled trial of tape specifically as a posture-correction method for appearance.

name: Dry needling / acupuncture

chain: Less tension in neck and shoulders
angle.text: People try needling of neck and upper-back trigger points to loosen tight muscles that they connect to rounded or hunched posture. Short-term pain relief has some evidence; effects on how posture looks have not been studied.

summary: Needling of tight muscles by clinicians; some short-term pain evidence, nothing for looks.
note: Rare serious injuries such as pneumothorax are reported; should be done by trained clinicians.
currentQuick:
Dry needling pushes a thin needle into tight muscle knots to ease pain. In posture and looksmaxxing talk it comes up as a way to loosen the neck, shoulders or jaw.
Reviews find some short-term pain benefit in certain conditions but small, low-quality studies. None examine appearance outcomes.
How it works: Practitioners say the needle disrupts trigger points and provokes a local twitch response that relaxes the muscle, and that it may alter nerve signaling. The exact mechanism is debated.
Risks and caveats: Soreness and bruising are common. Rare serious events such as pneumothorax or infection are reported, and practitioner scope of practice is disputed in several US states.
deepLead:
Dry needling is a technique in which a thin solid needle is inserted into muscle, most often at myofascial trigger points, to treat muscle pain. It is distinct in theory from acupuncture, though the two use similar needles and the relationship is disputed between professions .
In looksmaxxing and posture discussions it is mentioned as a way to release tight muscles in the neck, jaw and shoulders. It is a clinical pain-management technique and is not an established appearance treatment.
Systematic reviews describe short-term pain benefits in some conditions but note small, low-quality studies and methodological flaws, and the evidence for long-term benefit is limited .

name: Cervical traction

angle.text: Posture-focused users try cervical traction to ease a forward head position and improve neck and jaw-area profile. It is used in physiotherapy for nerve-root neck pain; its effect on posture appearance has not been tested.

summary: Neck pulling devices used in physio for nerve-root pain; no evidence for posture looks.
note: Clinical evidence for neck use is low quality; none for appearance.
currentQuick:
Cervical traction gently pulls on the neck, in a clinic or with a home device, to relieve pressure on neck nerves. Posture communities discuss it for neck curve and forward-head posture.
Research is about pain, not looks, and guideline evidence is described as low quality.
How it works: The proposed idea is that stretching the neck opens space between vertebrae and reduces nerve pressure. Some reviews report short-term pain relief when traction is added to physiotherapy.
Risks and caveats: The reviewed sources do not detail risks. Neck symptoms can have other causes, so traction is a clinical tool rather than an appearance treatment.
deepLead:
Cervical traction is the application of a pulling force to the neck, in a clinic or with a home device, intended to relieve pressure on spinal structures. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve root symptoms such as cervical radiculopathy .
In looksmaxxing and posture communities, neck traction devices are discussed as a way to improve neck curvature and forward-head posture. The sources reviewed contain no study of traction for appearance.
Guidelines for cervical traction rest on low-quality evidence, according to a summary of recent literature .

name: Spinal decompression therapy

angle.text: Spinal decompression is offered for disc pain, and some posture seekers hope it improves spinal alignment and stature. Small trials address back pain; appearance outcomes have not been investigated.

summary: Computerized table traction for disc pain; small trials for back pain, nothing for looks.
note: Evidence is for lumbar pain, not appearance; advertising claims have been questioned in the literature.
currentQuick:
Non-surgical spinal decompression uses a computerized table to gently stretch the spine, mainly marketed for disc herniation and nerve pain.
Small trials report pain and disc outcomes in lumbar patients. None examine posture or appearance.
How it works: Segmental distraction is said to reduce pressure on discs and nerve roots, and some studies measure changes in disc height or herniation size.
Risks and caveats: The reviewed sources do not detail adverse effects. A 2007 review questioned whether the literature supported the efficacy claims in advertising.
deepLead:
Non-surgical spinal decompression therapy is a table-based form of traction, usually computerized, offered by chiropractors and physical therapists for disc herniation and radiculopathy. The term spinal decompression also covers surgeries such as microdiscectomy and laminectomy that relieve pressure on nerves .
In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is mentioned for disc and spine concerns. It is a medical treatment for back pain and is not documented as an appearance procedure.
Small randomized trials report pain and disc outcomes in lumbar patients , while a 2007 review questioned whether the literature supported efficacy claims made in advertising .

name: Ergonomic setup (monitor at eye level)

chain: Less forward head, cleaner neck and jawline
angle.text: Posture communities raise monitors so the head stays upright rather than tilting down, with the goal of avoiding forward-head posture that affects the neck and jawline. The setup is standard ergonomics advice; its effect on looks has not been tested.

summary: Raising the screen to keep the head upright; sensible ergonomics, untested for looks.
note: No trials of monitor height or appearance outcomes among sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
This practice means raising your monitor so your head stays upright instead of tilting down. People discuss it as a way to avoid tech neck.
Ergonomics research focuses on workplace musculoskeletal symptoms. Evidence on workstation changes is mixed and nothing reviewed tests appearance.
How it works: The idea is that a neutral head position reduces sustained neck flexion and strain, and posture tools like RULA score neck angle as a risk factor.
Risks and caveats: No notable risks are described. Practice here is a low-cost workstation adjustment.
deepLead:
An ergonomic desk setup with the monitor at eye level is a posture practice in which people raise the screen so the head stays upright rather than tilting down. In posture and looksmaxxing communities it is described as a way to avoid so-called tech neck, a forward-head position associated with the neck and jawline.
Ergonomics is the scientific discipline that studies interactions between people and the systems they work in, aiming to improve well-being and performance; the term was used by Wojciech Jastrzębowski in 1857 and revived in English in 1949 .
The sources reviewed contain general ergonomics material and no trial of monitor height specifically, nor any examining appearance outcomes.

name: Phone at eye level / tech neck avoidance

angle.text: Looksmaxxing and posture circles recommend holding the phone high to avoid tech neck, linking it to a better neck line and jawline. Tech neck lacks an agreed definition, and the appearance link is based on anecdote.

summary: Keeping the phone high to avoid head-down posture; tech neck itself lacks an agreed definition.
note: No studies found testing the habit itself.
currentQuick:
This habit means lifting your phone toward eye level so your head does not tilt down. It is discussed to avoid tech neck and its alleged effect on neck and jaw look.
Research on tech neck is early and a 2023 review found no consensus definition. No study tests the habit.
How it works: The reasoning is biomechanical: a head held forward and down is said to load the neck more than an upright head.
Risks and caveats: No notable risks are described. Holding a phone higher is a behavioral change only.
deepLead:
Holding a phone at eye level to avoid tech neck, also called text neck, is a posture habit meant to prevent the head-down, forward-head position associated with prolonged device use. In looksmaxxing and posture communities it is linked to neck posture and jawline appearance.
A 2023 scoping review found that text neck is widely called a global epidemic but lacks a consensus definition across the peer-reviewed literature .
Related work has examined questionnaires on symptoms and preventive measures , skin changes sometimes labeled tech neck lines , and posture changes in skeletal remains .

name: Barefoot / minimalist shoes

chain: Thin flat shoes with wide toe box
angle.text: Fans of barefoot shoes say stronger feet and better mechanics carry up to better posture and lifting form, and so a better look. Early studies look at foot strength; links to posture or appearance are untested.

summary: Thin, flat, wide-toed shoes marketed as restoring natural foot function; evidence for foot strength is emerging, evidence for looks or posture is absent.
note: Running injuries are reported more often in the early period after switching.
currentQuick:
Barefoot or minimalist shoes have thin, flexible soles, little or no heel rise and often a wide toe box. In looksmaxxing forums they come up as a 'health-maxxing' habit said to rebuild foot muscles, improve posture and lifting form.
Research reviews report that minimalist footwear can increase foot muscle size and strength in healthy people, but no study has tested effects on posture or facial or body appearance.
How it works: By removing cushioning, heel elevation and arch support, the shoes let the foot flex and sense the ground more, which proponents say loads the foot's small muscles and encourages a forefoot or midfoot strike when running.
Risks and caveats: Reviews note more running injuries soon after switching and greater ankle and forefoot joint loading. Barefoot-style use also exposes feet to abrasions or punctures. Some forum users who also wear height-adding lifts worry about conflicting effects on the foot.
deepLead:
Barefoot or minimalist shoes are footwear designed to approximate walking or running barefoot. A 2015 consensus definition describes them as causing minimal interference with the natural movement of the foot, and a 2018 paper proposed objective criteria of a sole and upper weighing 200 g or less, a heel height of 20 mm or less and a heel-to-toe drop of 7 mm or less. Common features are a thin flexible sole, zero or near-zero drop, no arch support and a toe box wider than in conventional shoes; Vibram FiveFingers, Merrell Glove and Xero Prio are cited examples.
In looksmaxxing communities the shoes are mostly discussed as a posture and health topic rather than a direct beauty tool. Posters on looksmax.org argue that conventional shoes squeeze the toes and weaken foot muscles, and that wearing barefoot shoes improves foot mechanics, lifting form and, by extension, how one looks.
Published research on minimalist footwear concerns running economy, foot muscles and joint loading in healthy adults. A 2020 systematic review and later reviews summarised on Wikipedia report increased foot muscle size and strength, changes in Achilles tendon properties and mixed effects on joint loading, with early-period injuries more common. No study identified examines effects on posture, height or appearance.

name: Sleeping without a pillow

angle.text: Online posture advice says sleeping without a pillow reduces forward head posture, an idea traced in part to Joseph Pilates. Direct evidence is thin, and comfort and sleeping position largely shape what people experience.

summary: Resting the head flat on the mattress, pitched online as a fix for forward head posture; comfort and sleeping position decide the outcome and direct evidence is thin.
note: Side and back sleepers are often advised that going without a pillow can strain the neck.
currentQuick:
Sleeping without a pillow means lying with the head directly on a flat surface. In looksmaxxing circles it is suggested as a way to reduce forward head posture at night.
Available commentary says results depend mainly on sleep position: stomach sleepers are often described as suited to it, while side and back sleepers are generally advised to use a pillow. Direct controlled evidence for posture or appearance benefits is limited.
How it works: Proponents say a flat surface keeps the head level with the spine instead of propping it up. Sources describe the effect as depending on sleep position, shoulder width, neck length and mattress firmness.
Risks and caveats: Descriptions of the practice note possible neck overextension, stiffness or headaches in side sleepers and downward head tilt in back sleepers. Those with persistent pain or spinal conditions are advised to consult a clinician. One observational study linked lying flat with slightly lower eye pressure in glaucoma patients.
deepLead:
Sleeping without a pillow is the practice of resting the head directly on a mattress or other flat surface, with no head support or elevation. Some people reach it gradually by reducing the height of a thin pillow or folded towel over time. Accounts trace the idea in part to Joseph Pilates, who advised lying flat on a firm surface without a pillow in his book Return to Life Through Contrology.
In looksmaxxing communities the practice is raised as a way to counter forward head posture during sleep. A looksmax.org thread asks whether it is only about the spine or has further benefits, and one reply says there is not much difference and advises sleeping comfortably.
Commentary summarised on Grokipedia says that outcomes vary mainly by sleep position, that stomach sleepers may find it favourable, and that side and back sleepers are usually advised to use a pillow; it also states that direct scientific evidence is limited. That source is AI-generated and its claims are reported here cautiously.

name: Chestmaxxing / chest-out posture

angle.text: Chestmaxxing means standing with the chest open and raised, which visibly makes the upper body look broader and more confident while held. Open posture is generally read as confident, though the term itself has little formal study.

summary: Holding the chest open and raised as a posture habit; no studies of it as an appearance tactic, though open posture is generally read as confident.
currentQuick:
Chest-out posture is an open, upright stance with the chest raised and shoulders back, discussed in looksmaxxing as a way to look more confident and broader through the upper body.
No clinical study found tests it as an appearance intervention. Psychology references describe open posture as generally perceived as friendly and positive.
How it works: Practitioners hold the chest and shoulders in an expanded position; the term is also used for building chest size, which is a separate training topic.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are documented in the sources found. General guidance cited elsewhere says underlying medical conditions should be ruled out before reading much into posture.
deepLead:
Chestmaxxing or chest-out posture refers to carrying the chest open and raised as part of a posture-focused approach to appearance. Sources specific to the term are very limited.
A general psychology reference states that open posture, with a raised head and spread limbs, is often perceived as communicating a friendly and positive attitude, while closed posture is associated with an impression of detachment or disinterest. In one self-validation study cited there, participants in a confident posture rated their own qualities more favourably than those in a doubtful posture.
No published trial has tested chest-out posture as a way to change perceived attractiveness.

name: Posture Botox / muscle relaxants

angle.text: Some people consider botulinum toxin in neck or trapezius muscles for tension and a slimmer-looking neck and shoulder line. It is established for certain neck conditions; its use as a posture or looks tool is untested.

summary: Injecting botulinum toxin into neck or trapezius muscles for tension; established for some neck conditions, untested as a posture or looks tool.
note: Prescription-only; toxin spread can weaken unintended muscles.
currentQuick:
Botulinum toxin injected into neck or shoulder muscles is discussed as a way to ease tension. Botulinum toxin is established for conditions such as cervical dystonia and muscle spasticity.
No trial found tests it for posture correction or appearance in otherwise healthy people.
How it works: The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing temporary muscle weakness that reverses as nerves regenerate.
Risks and caveats: Adverse effects include spread to unintended muscles, weakness, swallowing trouble and allergic reactions, and the US FDA added boxed warnings about toxin spread in 2009. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and EU.
deepLead:
Posture Botox refers to the use of botulinum toxin injections in neck or trapezius muscles for tension. Botulinum toxin is an acetylcholine release inhibitor that causes flaccid paralysis of the injected muscle, with the effect slowly reversing as the nerve regenerates.
Its established medical uses include cervical dystonia, with type B approved by the FDA in 2000, and other muscle spasticity and spasm conditions; the Wikipedia article does not list trapezius or general neck tension as a specific indication. Many therapeutic uses are off-label in the US.
No study identified has tested botulinum toxin for improving posture or appearance in healthy people.

name: Scoliosis bracing / fusion surgery

angle.text: Bracing in growing teens and spinal fusion for severe curves are established orthopaedic treatments, and results include a straighter, more symmetrical back and torso. Surgery is sometimes recommended partly for cosmetic reasons in adulthood.

summary: Established orthopaedic treatments for spinal curvature; bracing aims to halt progression in growing teens, fusion straightens severe curves.
note: Surgery is major; brace outcomes depend heavily on wear compliance.
currentQuick:
Scoliosis bracing and spinal fusion are medical treatments for sideways spinal curvature. Bracing is used in growing patients to stop a curve worsening; fusion surgery is generally reserved for curves projected to pass about 45 to 50 degrees.
Appearance concerns are one factor: Wikipedia notes visible changes can affect teenagers' quality of life and cosmetic concerns are a key reason adults choose surgery.
How it works: A rigid torso brace such as a TLSO applies corrective force while the spine grows. Fusion joins vertebrae with metal instrumentation and bone graft to correct and hold the curve.
Risks and caveats: Surgery can be painful with a months-long recovery, and full straightening is usually not possible. Brace effectiveness depends on compliance, and braces have caused skin irritation and low self-esteem.
deepLead:
Bracing and spinal fusion are the two main treatments for progressive scoliosis. Bracing is used only while a patient is still growing, aiming to stop the curve progressing to the point where surgery is needed. Surgery is usually recommended for curves likely to progress beyond about 45 to 50 degrees, for curves interfering with breathing or sitting, and for curves that would be cosmetically unacceptable in adulthood.
For growing patients, curves under 20 degrees are monitored, 20 to 29 degrees are managed according to risk factors, and curves over 30 degrees generally prompt a bracing recommendation. The most common brace is the thoracolumbar sacral orthosis such as the Boston brace, typically worn 22 to 23 hours a day.
Wikipedia states that evidence shows bracing prevents curve progression, while its effect on quality of life, appearance or back pain is unclear.
